source.title: Applying sparse autoencoders to unlearn knowledge in language models
source.authors: Eoin Farrell; Yeu-Tong Lau; Arthur Conmy

page_placements.theme: Method and setting sensitivity of measured forgetting

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates a different, SAE-based intervention for reducing targeted knowledge and reports its effects on unrelated-task performance. It does not test recovery attacks against conventional unlearning.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own SAE interventions and an RMU comparison. The cited report that projecting out a direction can recover knowledge after RMU is prior work, not a result of this study, so it is not recorded as a row. Dense plot-only results are not assigned numerical values that the text does not state.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes and evaluates an SAE activation-clamping unlearning method on WMDP-bio. It reports forget accuracy and side effects, with RMU as a comparator. It runs no recovery attack of any kind: no fine-tuning, direction ablation, quantization or prompting. So its results do not bear on whether unlearning is shallow. The statement that knowledge stays in the weights follows from the method's design: it edits activations only. It is not an empirical finding. The only shallowness result mentioned, recovery from RMU by projecting out a direction, is cited prior work (Arditi & Chughtai). The study discusses the claim without testing it.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but it should add two points. First, the authors find that multi-feature SAE unlearning has similar or larger side effects than RMU. Second, they conclude that a large change to SAE training or the intervention is needed for SAE-based unlearning to succeed. They also note that because only activations change, the knowledge remains in the weights, though the method might still help for API-only access.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SAE feature activation interventions rather than the claim's gradient-ascent or Who's Harry Potter procedures; it also compares against RMU.
record.method_sensitivity: The effect depends on the clamp magnitude and selected feature(s); results also differ between gemma-2b-it and gemma-2-2b-it for random decoder vectors. The authors report that zero ablation has no noticeable effect, while negative clamping changes the answer on the illustrated question.

fits_no_version.finding: On gemma-2-2b-it, SAE feature clamping reaches WMDP-bio forget levels similar to RMU. It has larger side effects on selected MMLU questions but lower loss added on OpenWebText.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE activation-clamping unlearning has larger side effects on unrelated multiple-choice tasks than RMU at matched forget levels.

fits_no_version.finding: Zero-ablating SAE feature #9163 leaves the correct answer at probability above 0.99. Clamping it to about −18 to −20 flips the answer to C.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE-based unlearning needs negative clamping; zero ablation of features is ineffective.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing decoder vectors with random ones weakens unlearning on gemma-2-2b-it but not on gemma-2b-it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The role of specific SAE decoder directions in unlearning varies with the model and SAE.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix A: gemma-2b-it answers 39 of 172 always-correct WMDP-bio questions under all permutations without seeing the question. RMU-modified gemma answers 'A' on 62% of questions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: WMDP-bio multiple-choice accuracy partly reflects answer-format cues, which affects how unlearning should be measured.

record.problems: The paper does not test recovery attacks. Several key comparisons are presented in plots without numerical values in the text, and no uncertainty estimates are stated. The targeted WMDP-bio evaluation uses only questions the base model answered correctly under all 24 option permutations.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 5 contains multiple clamp-multiplier points for the 10-, 20-, and 50-feature SAE settings and RMU; individual plotted values are not stated in the text and are not separately transcribed. Figures 9 and 10 also show plot-only comparisons; Figure 10's qualitative comparison is included in R9.

untested.parts: No attack is run on either the SAE intervention or RMU, so robustness to recovery is untested. Forget and retain accuracy for the study's own method appear only in figures.
No direction ablation or other internal-edit recovery after unlearning. The 'knowledge remains in weights' statement holds by design and is not tested.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, other-language or in-context attack.
No method is claimed or tested to resist recovery attacks.

record.verdict_notes: The study is an unlearning-method evaluation, not a test of shallow unlearning. It does not count as a verdict-bearing study for any version. The reader's labels for A (limits_scope) and C (supports) are dropped. A's attack component and C's recovery component are never examined. The C statement is true by construction, and the cited RMU direction-projection result is prior work.

versions.untested_parts: The study evaluates targeted-knowledge accuracy and unrelated-task performance, but does not test whether simple attacks recover knowledge after unlearning.
No fine-tuning or relearning attack is tested.

It does not ablate a direction after an unlearning operation to test recovery, or test whether the finding generalizes to other unlearning methods. It states that its own SAE intervention changes activations, not weights, and that the knowledge remains in the weights.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language, or in-context recovery attack is tested.
No method is tested for resisting the recovery attacks in the claim.

relation.reason: It discusses superficial hiding versus real removal (intro), cites RMU's shallowness (Sec 4.2), and says its own method leaves the knowledge in the weights (conclusion). It tests none of this.

tranche.reason: Proposes and evaluates an SAE activation-clamping unlearning method, with RMU as a comparator. There is no relearning, direction-ablation, quantization or prompting attack on an unlearned model, so its results don't bear on versions A-F. The RMU shallowness point is cited from Arditi & Chughtai, not measured here.

source_check.notes: Both rows come from a case study of one question (#841) and one feature (#9163) on gemma-2b-it with a layer-9 SAE trained by the authors. They show the authors' own unlearning intervention working, not knowledge recovered after unlearning. RMU comparisons appear only in figures (Fig 5, Fig 9). No verdicts are on the record.

statements.correction: Optional context: gemma-2b-it, layer-9 SAE, one question (#841). The answer flips to C (> 0.99). Across permutations, 19 of 24 are unlearned.
statements.problem: None. It matches Section 3.2: ablating to 0 leaves A > 0.99, and a clamp of around -18 to -20 gives C > 0.99. It doesn't name the model or say it is one question, but it states nothing wrong.
